question: Pick's disease mainly affects which areas of the brain first?
explanation: Pick's disease zeroes in on the frontal and temporal parts of the brain, which handle our personality, behavior, and language. Spotting this early helps you understand why patients act differently long before memory issues start! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h1)

question: How does early Pick's disease usually look different from Alzheimer's disease?

options.A: Alzheimer's disease exclusively affects people under age fifty.
options.B: Alzheimer's disease causes rapid physical paralysis unlike Pick's disease.
options.C: Pick's disease alters behavior and personality first rather than memory.
options.D: Pick's disease begins with severe visual hallucinations.

explanation: You've got this! While Alzheimer's usually attacks memory first, Pick's disease changes how a person acts, talks to others, and handles their emotions right from the start. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h1)

question: Which abnormal protein builds up inside the nerve cells in Pick's disease?
explanation: Think of tau proteins as building blocks that go rogue and clump up inside the brain cells in Pick's disease. Knowing this pathology makes the rest of the topic much easier to master! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h2)

question: What exactly are 'Pick bodies' seen under a microscope in brain tissue?

options.A: Scars from previous traumatic head injuries
options.B: Deposits of calcium in the brain blood vessels
options.C: Clumps of abnormal tau protein inside nerve cells
options.D: Infections caused by bacteria in the spinal fluid

explanation: Pick bodies are just microscopic clumps of tangled tau protein. When neurons get weighed down by these clumps, they start to struggle and break down. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h2)

question: Which behavior do you typically see first in someone with Pick's disease?

options.A: Sudden tremors and rigidity in all four limbs
options.B: Inability to recognize familiar faces in mirrors
options.C: Loss of social inhibitions and personality changes
options.D: Complete loss of bladder and bowel control

explanation: Because the frontal lobe gets damaged, patients lose their 'social filter.' They might act very impulsively or say things they normally wouldn't, which is a classic sign to watch out for. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h3)

question: A patient with Pick's disease tries to eat paper wrappers and craves tons of sugar. How should you understand this?

options.A: It indicates the patient is suffering from severe iron-deficiency anemia.
options.B: It is a typical oral and dietary manifestation caused by temporal lobe damage.
options.C: It is a deliberate attempt by the patient to seek attention from staff.
options.D: It proves the patient has developed a secondary bacterial throat infection.

explanation: When the temporal lobe is affected, patients often develop strange eating habits, like craving sweets or trying to swallow non-food items. It's not for attention—it's the disease at work! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h3)

question: What is the classic scan finding for a patient with Pick's disease?

options.A: Atrophy localized to the frontal and temporal lobes
options.B: Swelling and inflammation throughout the cerebellum
options.C: Multiple blocked blood vessels in the deep brain
options.D: Enlargement of the occipital cortex exclusively

explanation: Spot on! 'Atrophy' just means shrinkage. Scans of Pick's patients clearly show shrinking right in the frontal and temporal areas of the brain. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h4)

question: Why can diagnosing Pick's disease be tricky in the beginning?

options.A: Its behavioral symptoms can be mistaken for psychiatric disorders.
options.B: Standard MRI scanners cannot image the frontal lobes clearly.
options.C: Routine blood tests can easily confuse it with normal aging.
options.D: Patients usually retain perfect memory until the final days.

explanation: Because the very first signs are personality changes and apathy, doctors sometimes mistake it for depression, anxiety, or mental health issues rather than a brain disease. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h4)

question: What is the main goal of medical treatment for Pick's disease?

options.A: Restoring lost brain tissue in the frontal lobe
options.B: Reversing the underlying cellular tau accumulation
options.D: Managing behavioral symptoms and improving comfort

explanation: Since we can't cure or reverse the disease yet, our nursing care focuses on keeping the patient comfortable, calm, and managing tough behavioral symptoms. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h5)

question: Why are standard Alzheimer's drugs usually avoided or used carefully in Pick's disease?

options.A: They accelerate memory loss within the first week of use.
options.B: They interfere with routine blood pressure medications.
options.C: They do not target the underlying pathology and can worsen agitation.
options.D: They cause immediate and permanent paralysis of the lower limbs.

explanation: Alzheimer's medications don't help frontotemporal issues and can actually make behavioral outbursts worse. It's a great clinical pearl to remember for your exams! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h5)

question: A patient with Pick's disease tries to wander out of the ward wearing only a hospital gown. What is your best immediate nursing action?

options.A: Apply soft wrist restraints immediately to prevent wandering attempts.
options.B: Gently redirect the patient toward a quiet lounge area with a familiar activity.
options.C: Explain firmly and logically why leaving the ward is dangerous for health.
options.D: Lock the patient inside the hospital room until visiting hours are over.

explanation: Redirection is your best friend here! Arguing or reasoning usually fails because of brain damage, but gently steering them to a cozy spot keeps them safe without a fight. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h6)

question: What is a major safety risk for patients with Pick's disease due to temporal lobe changes?

options.A: Developing sudden and severe bone fractures from walking
options.B: Inability to feel pain when touching hot stove surfaces
options.C: Sudden loss of hearing making them unable to hear fire alarms
options.D: Attempting to eat non-food objects or dangerous substances

explanation: Because of changes in how they experience things orally, these patients might try to chew or swallow harmful objects. Keeping hazardous items out of reach is a crucial nursing priority! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h6)

question: Why is caring for someone with Pick's disease often so emotionally draining for families?

options.A: The disease progresses much faster than any other form of dementia.
options.B: Patients require constant surgical procedures throughout the illness.
options.C: Family members are legally required to pay for all hospital care.
options.D: The loss of personality and social filter can feel emotionally rejecting.

explanation: It hurts deeply when a loved one changes personality, loses their warmth, or acts out of character. Families need plenty of empathy and support from nurses to cope with this grief. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h7)

question: When is the best time to talk about end-of-life wishes and care planning with the family?

options.A: As early in the disease trajectory as possible
options.B: When the patient develops sudden aspiration pneumonia
options.C: Immediately after the final post-mortem examination
options.D: Only after the patient becomes completely mute and bedbound

explanation: Having these conversations early lets the patient share what they want while they still can, making future medical choices much easier for everyone involved. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h7)
